awd_titl_txt: DDRIG: Interplay between Embodiment and Technoscience
awd_abstract_narration:
This research examines how visions of a global “information age” have changed ways of conceptualizing and experiencing human potential.    The dissertation study uses three case studies to examine the interplay between embodiment and technoscience. This work addresses broader contemporary concerns about how information technologies have intimately changed the way people understand themselves and their connection with their surroundings. The results of this project are communicated through conference presentations, journal publications, and undergraduate teaching.

Combining state archives with records from published books, journals, media reports, laboratory reports, and memoirs, the project examines how the information revolution also entailed a transformation of human bodily understanding. The study asks: 1. How did medico-scientific and technological practices generate new visions of human capability and potential, and how did these intersect with visions of technoscientific modernization? 2. How have theories such as information theory, systems science, and cybernetics become localized and how do they interact with vernacular medical knowledge to shape new understandings of the human body as an informational entity?  To address these questions, the project combines theoretical frameworks from Science and Technology Studies with archival research.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
This grant supported dissertation research for Yue Zhao under the supervision of Dr. Rachel Prentice at the Department of Science & Technology Studies at Cornell University. Research on this grant explored how an information revolution also entailed changes in understanding the human body’s capacity and capability in the late twentieth century. The project contributes to public understanding of the politics behind information technology by offering historical context for how the relationships between humans and machines took shape.

The project focused on how natural and social scientists, medical professionals, government officials, and citizens in China’s reform era explored research on cultivating and developing human bodily capacities—such as how to sense and pay attention in everyday life—amidst anxieties and concerns over an information revolution around the globe. In the early 1980s, officials and intellectuals questioned whether existing knowledge, economic structures, and people’s physical abilities could keep pace with a fast-approaching information society. Out of these debates emerged the idea that the human body itself might be understood as a kind of living information machine, capable of being modeled, trained, and optimized. The project draws on multiple forms of archives, including institutional records, published monographs and reports, news reports, and handbooks to uncover this history. 

The dissertation argues that this scientific and technological vision of human potential carried political ambitions. The drive to unlock citizens’ hidden bodily capacities was tied to a larger effort to redefine the nation’s identity, repositioning it as a center of scientific discovery and technological innovation in the late Cold War world. Preliminary findings also contribute to broader contemporary concerns about how information metaphors have sunk deep into the human psyche and physicality, changing the way people understand themselves and their relationship with technological surroundings. 

In undertaking this work, the award supported archival research in China and the presentation of findings at an international conference in Canada. Research conducted under this award also supported the writing of multiple dissertation chapters, a conference paper, and an academic article currently under review.
